newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan faces more problems over islands dispute.
newsitem.headline: Japan faces more problems over islands dispute.

text.p: The planting of Chinese and Taiwanese flags on a disputed island on Monday is a new headache for the Japanese government in an increasingly bitter territorial dispute it wishes would just go away.

Japan voiced "regret" and called for calm when Taiwan and Hong Kong activists pierced a Japanese maritime cordon at dawn on Monday, swam ashore and hoisted the flags on an East China Sea island in a challenge to Tokyo's claim of sovereignty.

Analysts said Japan, locked in separate territorial disputes with Russia and South Korea, has no option but to stand firm in its acrimonious row with China and Taiwan over ownership of the uninhabited islands in the East China Sea.

"If Japan softens or reverses its basic policy on the Senkaku Islands, that would put it in a very difficult position to deal with the separate issues involving Russia and South Korea," political analyst Minoru Morita said.
Japan is embroiled in a thorny dispute with Russia over a string of four small islands off northern Japan since Soviet troops seized them in the closing days of World War Two.
The dispute has stopped Tokyo, which calls the islands the Northern Territories, from providing large-scale financial aid to Russia or signing a formal peace treaty with Moscow.
And a long-dormant sovereignty dispute between Japan and South Korea was rekindled in February when Japan prepared to designate a 200-nautical mile exclusive economic zone around its shores.
The expanded zone would put two tiny, uninhabited islands in the Sea of Japan, called Tokdo by South Korea and Takeshima by Japan, within Tokyo's sovereignty.

Tokyo has claimed the islands since 1905 when it signed, some historians say forced, an agreement with Korea that paved the way for its often brutal colonial rule over the Korean Peninsula from 1910 to 1945.
Korea says its claim to the islands dates back to 512.
Japan established diplomatic relations with South Korea in 1965 but many Koreans still harbour bitter memories of Japan's 35 years of colonial rule.
Tokyo maintained a low profile on Monday when Taiwan and Hong Kong activists landed on one of the East China Sea islets and hoisted flags of both communist China and Nationalist-ruled Taiwan.
"The question is how all parties concerned can calm down to prevent the uproar from spreading further," Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told reporters.
He said Japan would calmly deal with the dispute in a way that does not aggravate Tokyo's relations with China and Taiwan, while clearly asserting its claim to the islands.

Last Friday, Japan announced it would not recognise a lighthouse built on one of the islands by a right-wing group, a key factor that rekindled the dispute over the islands, known as the Senkakus in Japanese and the Diaoyus in Chinese.
Rivals China and Taiwan, which separately challenge Japan's claim to the uninhabited islands, condemned the construction of the lighthouse and demanded its immediate removal.
Japan's claim dates to 1895 when it defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories. Tokyo says the issue is not open for discussion.
China has claimed sovereignty over the islands for centuries.
Taiwan has no diplomatic ties with Japan, which only recognises Beijing's Communist government.
Political analyst Morita said one way Japan could try to avert a diplomatic crisis would be to conclude fishing agreements with the countries concerned.
"If not, they will bash each other over the territorial dispute with no end in sight," he said.
